It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing a world where political powers grow cold toward the Gospel and seek to claim authority that belongs to the King alone, and I must ask you with a gentle heart: why do you ask after the boundaries between civil authority and the headship of Christ in this hour? [13, 253, 1431, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by the sight of “savage wolves” who use human law as a “scourge” against the faithful, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the rise and fall of every nation? [13, 20, 39, 262, 1143, 1374, 1379, 1425, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many seek “diplomatic relations” with a culture that “mocks, vilifies, and censures” the Scriptures to avoid the “scars” of the cross, we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “record of history” by reminding us that our “citizenship is in heaven” [11, 25, 28, 38, 120, 132, 203, 334, 1197, 1313, 1317, 1320, 1426, 1503, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the tension between church and state is not an “administrative anomaly” but is subject to the “decree from God” who “raises up kings, then pulls them from their thrones when they have served His administration” [15, 29, 68, 237, 249, 694, 1143, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Prophet and the Law of the King (Israel)**

**Verse**
“ ‘Now it shall be, when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book, from the one before the priests, the Levites. And it shall be with him, and he shall read it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God and be careful to observe all the words of this law and these statutes, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brethren’ ” (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). [690, 703, 1229, 1251, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Scriptures reveal that in the ancient theocracy, the king was never an absolute law unto himself; he was “subject to the Word of God” and commanded to maintain a “fear of the LORD” to prevent his heart from being “lifted up” in pride [703, 1232, 1438, 1503, Conversation History]. Reformed theology—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that “God rules the universe” and any human ruler who “rejected the word of the LORD” was Himself rejected by the King of Kings, as seen when Samuel rebuked Saul (1 Samuel 15:23, “ ‘Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He also has rejected you from being king’ ”) [10, 694, 886, 1078, 1183, 1533, Conversation History]. Even the most powerful monarchs were reminded that “the judgment is God’s,” and their primary duty was to ensure “justice for all” rather than their own “political status” (Deuteronomy 1:17; John 11:48) [130, 689, 1172, 1255, 1316, 1365, 1473, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not look for some other fountain of knowledge” in “political maneuvering” to save a nation; instead, recognize that a leader’s “sole objective” should be to “ascribe greatness to our God” (Deuteronomy 32:3) [51, 59, 123, 706, 1406, 1503, 1623, Conversation History]. When a ruler “perverts justice” or “takes a bribe,” they are committing a “wicked deed” that God “will not at all acquit” (Exodus 23:7–8; Proverbs 17:15) [177, 700, 1190, 1240, 1267, 1317, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Theocratic Shadows**
In the **ancient Jewish context**, civil and religious law were often intertwined because Israel was a “holy nation” under a “theocratic” administration where “national greatness” was a “temporal sign” of favor [409, 718, 943, 1237, 1249, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “victory,” showing that while the kingly prototype was found in Moses and David, the true “Prophet-King” is Jesus, whose rule is mediated through the “Spirit of truth” rather than a physical throne in this age (Hebrews 1:8) [125, 707, 828, 934, 1309, 1311, 1418, 1503, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: Sovereignty in the Horrible Pit (The Exile)**

**Verse**
“ ‘And in the days of these kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever’ ” (Daniel 2:44). [20, 24, 747, 1383, 1493, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
During the Exile, God demonstrated that His authority remains “absolute” even when His people are in a “horrible pit” under “pagan Babylonian society” [3, 25, 1143, 1440, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition notes that God “harnesses the deeds of the wicked”—even the “massacre” and “plunder” of armies like the Chaldeans—to accomplish His “good and perfect ends” (Isaiah 46:10, “ ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will do all My pleasure’ ”) [5, 64, 917, 1132, 1143, 1383, 1397, 1493, 1515, 1567, 1616, Conversation History]. Every earthly despot who “thinks themselves much better than they really are” is eventually told, “ ‘You have been weighed on the scales and found deficient’ ” (Daniel 5:27) [11, 15, 26, 37, 914, 1061, 1143, 1402, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Trade in your worry for trust,” for though “earthly kingdoms go the way of all flesh,” the “Lord has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19) [15, 21, 26, 29, 39, 42, 68, 94, 201, 1143, 1340, 1408, 1515, 1532, 1572, Conversation History]. You must “discipline your mind” to recognize that “not one human sinner or demonic power will ever succeed in his rebellion” against the Sovereign [11, 15, 68, 116, 249, 1143, 1406, 1532, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Civil vs. Divine Decrees**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, God used “hostile nations” as a “rod of My anger” to discipline His people, but He still held those nations “responsible for their own rejection” of the truth (Isaiah 10:5; Romans 9:22) [66, 650, 866, 917, 1110, 1130, 1133, 1316, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “repose of the soul,” showing that we do not wait for a “storage city” of human building, but for a “city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10) [25, 142, 1251, 1257, 1313, 1426, 1529, 1646, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: Rendering to Caesar and the Higher King**

**Verse**
“And He said to them, ‘Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ ” (Matthew 22:21). [903, 996, Conversation History]. “Jesus answered, ‘My kingdom is not of this world. If My kingdom were of this world, My servants would fight, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now My kingdom is not from here’ ” (John 18:36). [17, 28, 1329, 1431, 1529, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—echoed by **John MacArthur**—teaches that while the state is “ordained by God” as a “minister to you for good” to “punish evildoers,” its jurisdiction is limited to the “physical and moral universe” (Romans 13:1–4; 1 Peter 2:14) [15, 75, 298, 892, 1018, 1143, 1169, 1184, 1329, 1342, 1422, 1473, 1532, 1720, Conversation History]. Because we were “bought at a price” and bear the “image of God,” our “whole identity” and “highest allegiance” belong to the King who “upholds all things by the word of His power” (1 Corinthians 6:20; Hebrews 1:3) [12, 13, 31, 42, 101, 254, 257, 309, 1138, 1262, 1315, 1406, 1503, 1670, Conversation History]. Christ’s instruction on taxes acknowledges the state's “administrative authority,” but His claim that His kingdom is “not from here” establishes that the church’s “worship and governance” cannot be “subjugated” to a “politician” [61, 293, 298, 694, 1329, 1418, 1503, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity” by obeying the law in mundane matters, for “this is the will of God” (1 Timothy 2:2; 1 Peter 2:15) [21, 60, 63, 76, 77, 79, 82, 93, 116, 893, 925, 1017, 1105, 1284, 1473, 1515, 1709, Conversation History]. However, you must “refuse to yield submission” to any authority that tries to “tamper with or attempt to tone down the gospel,” for “your life is not your own” (Galatians 2:5; 1 Corinthians 6:19) [12, 19, 101, 722, 1043, 1092, 1138, 1144, 1262, 1316, 1406, 1431, 1503, 1528, 1638, 1670, 1720, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Revision of Warfare**
Under the **Mosaic Law**, “military skill” and the “sword” were tools of the theocratic state, but Christ’s teaching **revises** the “warfare” of His people [292, 684, 1245, 1313, 1519, Conversation History]. He commanded, “ ‘Put your sword in its place,’ ” revealing that the “church militant” conquers “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” rather than through “carnal weaponry” (Matthew 26:52; Revelation 12:11) [11, 21, 32, 92, 440, 1113, 1313, 1325, 1327, 1402, 1491, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

### **Section 4: The Sanhedrin and the Apostolic Mandate**

**Verse**
“But Peter and the other apostles answered and said: ‘We ought to obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus whom you murdered by hanging on a tree. Him God has exalted to His right hand to be Prince and Savior’ ” (Acts 5:29–31). [48, 882, 914, 1130, 1146, 1176, 1205, 1247, 1249, 1256, 1300, 1431, 1529, 1720, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The “highest religious court in Israel,” the Sanhedrin, was exposed as “corrupt” and “unjust” when they sought to “silence” the message of the cross to protect their “influence over the common people” [130, 197, 198, 1316, 1365, 1422, 1720, Conversation History]. The apostles’ response establishes a “binding and authoritative mandate” for the church: when human laws forbid the “herald, proclaim[ing], or speaking publicly” of the Savior, the believer must stand with “boldness” because “the Father has given Him authority over us” [11, 15, 68, 125, 241, 284, 530, 785, 912, 1130, 1316, 1432, 1503, 1528, 1720, Conversation History]. To “obey God rather than men” is not an act of “rebellion” in the carnal sense, but an act of “loyalty” to the “One who has the right to rule and reign” [15, 19, 41, 50, 76, 1130, 1143, 1341, 1529, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “be bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God in much conflict,” knowing that “the Word of God is not chained” (1 Thessalonians 2:2; 2 Timothy 2:9) [11, 25, 41, 51, 76, 91, 123, 767, 1081, 1406, 1420, 1431, 1461, 1503, 1504, 1646, 1670, 1720, Conversation History]. Recognize that “cowardice and authentic faith are antithetical,” and your “sole objective” is to “testify to the gospel of the grace of God” even if you are “commit[ed] to prison” (Acts 20:24; 8:3) [11, 27, 31, 130, 323, 765, 782, 824, 843, 861, 975, 1022, 1069, 1296, 1406, 1503, 1623, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Ecclesiastical Usurpation**
In the **ancient context**, “religious leaders” often “usurped” Christ’s authority by “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Matthew 15:9) [111, 1002, 1431, 1503, 1507, 1545, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** the structure of the household of faith, revealing that “Jesus Christ alone is the head of the church,” and any “pope,” “politician,” or “pastor” who tries to “usurp the title” is a “spirit of fraud” [279, 284, 285, 286, 289, 293, 412, 415, 1233, 1314, 1411, 1418, 1528, 1627, 1636, 1720, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: • Upon seeing the magnitude of God’s holiness, Job repented and retracted all that he had foolishly said (Job 42:5–6). • Standing in the presence of God’s holiness, Isaiah pronounced a curse on himself, “Woe is me, for I am ruined!” (Isa. 6:5). • Habakkuk trembled at the voice of holy God (Hab. 3:16).  • The restored remnant feared the Lord when they heard His holy word spoken by the prophet Haggai (Hag. 1:12).  • During our Lord’s earthly ministry, the disciples often came face- to-face with His power and holiness. On one occasion when they were crossing the Sea of Galilee, a storm appeared. Although they were afraid of the storm, they feared greatly (literally “feared a great fear”) when Jesus calmed the storm (Mark 4:41). They became much more fearful of the presence and power of God than they were of the deadly storm. Stained by the sin of unbelief, Peter implored his sinless Lord to depart from him (Luke 5:8). John, James, and Peter fell on their faces and were exceedingly afraid when they heard the voice of God (Matt. 17:6).

The notion of a lower tier of prophets who are frequently inaccurate in their prophetic declarations is completely absent from the New Testament record. The New Testament nowhere suggests that prophets in the church were to be held to a lesser standard than their Old Testament counterparts. In fact, the evidence indicates exactly the opposite. New Testament prophets, no matter what church congregation they were part of, were held to the very same standard as those used...the very same standards as those used in the Old Testament. So, for starters, the New Testament refers to both Old Testament and New Testament prophets using the exact same terminology. There is no distinction in the way the New Testament talks about Old Testament prophets, or New Testament prophets.

At present, the kingdom is a spiritual dominion, not an earthly geopolitical realm. Jesus described the current state of the kingdom as intangible and invisible: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation; nor will they say, ‘See here!’ or ‘See there!’ For indeed, the kingdom of God is within [or among] you” (Luke 17:20–21). He also said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). This is not the full and final expression of Christ’s kingdom, of course. The earthly culmination of the kingdom awaits His bodily return. Then all “the kingdoms of this world [will] become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign forever and ever!” (Rev. 11:15). The first phase of that eternal rule is the thousand-year reign of the Lord Jesus on earth promised in Revelation 20:1–7. That is followed by the creation of the new heaven and the new earth over which His eternal reign continues (Rev. 21:1–8).

That was undoubtedly a major shock to everyone who heard it. Say what you will about the Pharisees’ hypocrisy and hidden wickedness, they had nevertheless elevated obedience to the law’s external commands to an unprecedented level. If God graded human behavior on a curve, the Pharisees would have been at the head of the class. But Jesus was pointing out that God doesn’t adjust the scale of righteousness to accommodate human failure. His own righteousness is flawlessly perfect, and to lower that standard even slightly in order to accommodate our sin would make Him unholy.

Believers can therefore be described as those for whom there remains “no condemnation” (Rom. 8:1). They have been sealed with the Holy Spirit, signifying the irrevocable nature of God’s divine guarantee. They are “protected by the power of God” (1 Peter 1:5), such “that He who began a good work in [them] will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:6). That is why Paul could pray for the Thessalonians, “Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass” (1 Thess. 5:23–24; emphasis added). He would echo those same words in his second letter to that same church: “The Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen and protect you from the evil one” (2 Thess. 3:3). Jude similarly concluded his epistle with this triumphant doxology: “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to make you stand in the presence of His glory blameless with great joy, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen” (vv. 24–25; emphasis added).

Every believer, whether slave or free, has a Master in heaven. He is a perfect and impartial Judge, and one day we will each stand before Him to give an account. The certainty of that future reality emboldened Paul to preach the gospel no matter the consequences. After all, he had been appointed to do so by the commandment of God Himself (Titus 1:3). Though he would often be rejected and persecuted, Paul was far more concerned with obeying his divine calling than with gaining man’s approval. Only one thing mattered— pleasing the Master.
